hints: Look carefully at where your graph crosses the zero line on the y-axis. What sucrose concentration gives no overall mass change, and where does $0.45 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ sit compared to that point?

Remember water always moves by osmosis from higher (less negative) water potential to lower (more negative) water potential. If the cylinder loses mass at $0.45 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, which side started with the higher water potential and what must happen to water in the vacuole?
walkthrough:
**Find the isotonic point from the graph**

Look for 0% change in mass. That happens at about $0.3 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.

This tells you the cell sap inside the cells has about the same water potential as $0.3 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ sucrose solution. No net osmosis happens there.

**Compare 0.45 to the isotonic point**

$0.45 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ is to the right of $0.3 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ on the x-axis. It is a more concentrated sucrose solution.

More solute means a lower, more negative water potential:
$$\text{water potential of } 0.45 \text{ solution} < \text{water potential of cell cytoplasm}$$
So the cytoplasm at the start was less negative (higher) than the $0.45 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ solution.

**Predict water movement and vacuole change**

Water moves down the water potential gradient, from the cytoplasm out into the $0.45 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ solution.

The graph confirms this because at 0.4 and 0.5 the percentage change is negative, so mass is lost. Losing water means the vacuole shrinks, so its volume decreased. That matches row A.

options.A: Correct. Cytoplasm is like 0.3 solution, so it is less negative than 0.45 solution, water leaves by osmosis and vacuole volume decreases.
options.B: Water potential part is right, but water leaving cannot make the vacuole swell and increase in volume.
options.C: Vacuole decrease is right, but if cytoplasm were more negative than the solution, water would enter, not leave.
options.D: Both parts are reversed. More negative cytoplasm would gain water and the vacuole would increase, but the graph shows mass loss at 0.45.
